a subset of electrodes in an ECoG grid showed planar, rotational, or concentric waves (Figure 9,
Supplementary Figures 9-18).

If the size of the ECoG grid is small, such as the 64 or 84 grids in our dataset, there is a
possibility that the detected planar waves could represent segments of larger rotational waves.
Therefore, the number of rotational waves that we have detected in our dataset could potentially
be undercounted. Future studies with much larger ECoG arrays across many individuals are
needed for a more accurate assessment of the number of rotational waves and their functional
role during various memory tasks.

Validating CICA using simulations
In addition to statistical validation on the experimental data using shuffling, we have also carried
out four types of simulations to validate our proposed CICA approach to confirm its sensitivity
to extract expected wave patterns and demonstrate specificity to reject negative results in the
absence of such patterns.

Simulation 1, Sensitivity test, single wave patterns: In this simulation, we test the sensitivity
of our framework where we feed-in known traveling wave patterns and then test the robustness
of the CICA framework against noise. We first simulated a plane wave using an 8*8 electrode
grid and added Gaussian random noise to generate multiple trials (100 in total) and then passed
these into our CICA algorithm to test how well our algorithm is able to estimate the wave
pattern. We generated activation functions or weights from a uniform distribution. To quantify,
we calculated the root-mean-squared-error (RMSE) between the ground-truth pattern and the
estimated pattern by the CICA approach and we repeated this procedure from low to high signal-
to-noise ratio (SNR). RMSE for this simulation and all subsequent simulations below was
calculated by taking the root of the sum of squared differences of the activation functions
estimated by CICA and the activation functions in the original data that we simulated. This
demonstrates the ability of CICA to not only reconstruct the modes present in the original data,
but also the degree of representativeness of the individual modes timepoint-by-timepoint. If the
activation functions estimated by CICA match the activation functions in the original data
timepoint-by-timepoint, then it can be claimed that CICA has high sensitivity. Additionally, we
also tested the robustness of our CICA approach using rotational wave, source wave, and
complex wave patterns.

Results from this analysis are summarized in Supplementary Figure 4A, which showed that the
performance of the CICA approach improved as SNR increased, with near-perfect reconstruction
of the underlying traveling wave patterns at higher SNR values. Moreover, the performance of
the different wave shapes such as planar, source, rotational, and complex waves were very
similar, demonstrating the ability of the CICA approach to robustly estimate a diverse range of
wave patterns. Simulation 1 demonstrates the sensitivity of the CICA method for a single wave-
type and CICA is able to reconstruct the waveforms for each individual timepoints, in addition to
reconstructing the shape of the waveform, i.e., the mode.

Simulation 2, Sensitivity test, multiple wave patterns: In this simulation, we test the
sensitivity of our framework for identifying and distinguishing combinations of traveling wave
patterns, i.e., multiple modes, in the presence of noise. For this, we simulated planar+source,
planar+rotational, planar+complex, and planar+source+rotational wave patterns. We generated
the activation functions for each type of wave shape from a uniform distribution. We again added
Gaussian random noise to generate multiple trials and then passed these into our CICA algorithm
to test how well our algorithm is able to separate multiple wave patterns. To quantify, we
calculated the root-mean-squared-error between the ground-truth pattern and the estimated
pattern by the CICA approach for all wave shapes and we repeated this procedure from low to
high SNR.

Results from this analysis are summarized in Supplementary Figure 4B, which showed that the
performance of the CICA approach improved as SNR increased, similar to results from
Simulation 1, with near-perfect reconstruction of the underlying traveling wave patterns at higher
SNR values, demonstrating the ability of the CICA approach to robustly estimate the underlying
wave patterns when multiple traveling waves are simultaneously present. For example, if the
degree of representativeness of the rotational wave-type is high at a specific time-point, then
CICA is accurately able to reconstruct this waveform at that individual time-point, and therefore
the RMSE is close to zero at reasonably high SNR in our simulations.

Simulation 3, Specificity test: We also tested the specificity of the CICA method in the
presence of spatially autocorrelated signal whose spatial autocorrelation matches to those in the
spatial and verbal experimental data. We considered a rotational wave. Note that these rotational
waves were ubiquitous in our experimental data and the spatial autocorrelation of the rotational
wave matches to those in the experimental data. We also created spatially circularly shifted
versions of the original rotational wave: vertically shifted, horizontally shifted and both
vertically and horizontally shifted versions (Supplementary Figure 5). Note that the spatial
autocorrelation of all these circularly shifted waves is the same as the original rotational wave,
although the specific structure is now destroyed. We separately gave these circularly shifted
waves and also the original rotational wave as inputs to the CICA method. For the circularly
shifted waves, we created 500 permutations of the circular shift and for each permutation, we
generated 50 trials by adding Gaussian random noise to the traveling waves and passing them to
the CICA method as input. This analysis revealed that CICA cannot reconstruct the original
rotational wave anymore after using the circularly shifted versions. The error magnitude when
the original wave is given as input to the CICA method is significantly lower than the
distribution of the error magnitudes when the circularly shifted waves are given as input to CICA
(p < 0.001). This analysis strongly demonstrates the ability of CICA to show negative results in
the absence of any specific shape of wave patterns.

Simulation 4, Joining tests of sensitivity and specificity: This test assesses the joint ability of
our framework to distinguish individual trials that showed real versus no waves, within an
individual dataset. For this, we simulated rotational waves and planar+source+rotational wave
patterns. The performance of other wave patterns such as planar waves and source waves was
similar to the rotational wave pattern and hence omitted. For the input, half of the trials consisted
of the given wave pattern (rotational or planar+source+rotational) and the other half consisted of
no wave (zero signal, corresponds to zero weights or activation functions). We then calculated
the detection percentage of our CICA approach, i.e., we calculated the percentage of trials our
CICA approach is able to correctly identify the presence or absence of the wave patterns and we
repeated this procedure from low to high SNR.

This analysis revealed that the CICA correctly estimates both the presence and absence of wave
patterns (Supplementary Figure 4C). For the rotational wave shape, CICA is able to achieve
near-perfect detection accuracy at > ~ 15 dB SNR and for the planar+source+rotational case,
CICA is able to achieve near-perfect detection accuracy at > ~ 20 dB SNR, for both the
sensitivity and specificity tests, demonstrating the ability of the CICA to extract the expected
wave patterns and also demonstrate negative results in the absence of such patterns. Simulation 4
demonstrates both the sensitivity and specificity of the CICA method. Simulation 4 demonstrates
that the time-points where there was a wave present, CICA is able to accurately reconstruct both
the shape and the degree of representativeness of that waveform at that individual time-point. On
the other hand, CICA is also able to estimate the value of zero activation function with high
accuracy at a given time-point where there was no wave, indicating that CICA can produce null
result when there are no waves. Furthermore, in the case where we simulated multiple
waveforms in equal contribution such as the “planar+source+rotational” case, the CICA method
was able to reconstruct all of these three waveforms in equal contribution. Therefore, Simulation
4 strongly demonstrates both the sensitivity and specificity of the CICA method.

We would like to clarify that the individual time-points in our simulations correspond to the
individual stable epochs in the experimental data. The shape of the traveling waves changes from
one stable epoch to the next stable epoch, therefore the wave shapes also change from one task
(for example, encoding) to the other (for example, retrieval). The CICA method is able to capture
the variability of the changes in the wave shapes by using the activation functions whose value
dynamically changes across different stable epochs and task periods, indicating the sensitivity
and specificity of the CICA method. Similarly, in the simulations, the CICA method is able to
capture the presence or absence of waveforms or the degree of representativeness of the
waveforms by estimating the dynamic or time-varying activation functions. Since, in our
simulations, we simulated planar, spiral, and concentric waves, which were ubiquitous in our
experimental data and whose spatial autocorrelation is highly similar to the experimental data,
our simulations therefore very strongly support the claims in our experimental data as well.

Statistical analysis of the relation between traveling waves and behavior
(i) Identifying significant modes in CICA
To estimate the number of significant modes in the CICA output for each cluster, we compared
the variance explained for each mode with the theoretical variance threshold 100/n, where n is
the number of electrodes in an ECoG grid. This theoretical variance corresponds to the variance
of each mode if the total variance (100%) is equally distributed among all modes. Because of the
spatial structure of traveling waves, some modes will explain more variance compared to the
other modes in the empirical data (Figure 4E). We additionally shuffled the electrodes in each
cluster and recalculated the variance distribution across modes and confirmed that the shuffled
variance for all modes converged to the theoretical variance threshold of 100/n.

(ii) Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA)
To identify how traveling wave patterns related to behavior, we directly compared the weights
estimated from the CICA procedure above between encoding, retrieval, navigation, etc. periods
in the TH task and between the English letters in the ST task, for each mode using multivariate
analysis of variance (MANOVA). MANOVA was used because the weights were complex. We
statistically distinguished weights corresponding to different behavioral states using the
following model: Real + Imag ~ States, where Real and Imag are the real and imaginary parts of
the weights respectively and States are encoding, retrieval, navigation, etc. in the TH task or
letters “B”, “G”, etc. in the ST task. We used this model for each mode and applied FDR-
corrections for multiple comparisons (p < 0.05) across all modes and oscillation clusters.
Statistical significance from the MANOVA would indicate that traveling waves shift their
direction and/or strength to form distinct directional patterns which can distinguish different
behavioral states. We designated an oscillation cluster to be significant if at least one of the
modes from the CICA for that cluster showed statistical significance in MANOVA. Moreover,
we also repeated our MANOVA analysis by shuffling the labels of the different behavioral states
such as encoding, retrieval, etc. and built a histogram from these shuffles (f-statistics) against
which we compared the empirical data. This analysis revealed that all our MANOVA results
were still statistically significant (p’s < 0.05).

(iii) Robustness of traveling waves at the individual epoch level
We conducted surrogate analysis to test the significance of the estimated stable epochs (see
Identification of stable epochs section above) and whether the observed stable epochs are beyond
chance levels. For each time-point, we shuffled the trial labels so that the temporal contiguity
within a given trial is destroyed and also the electrodes, so that the spatial topography for the
corresponding behavioral state is destroyed, and then ran the stable epoch analysis using
identical methodology as above. In this way, we built a surrogate distribution by aggregating all
time-points corresponding to these shuffled stable epochs against which we then compared the
aggregated time-points from the empirical stable epochs (p < 0.05).

Additionally, we also carried out statistical tests based on spatial autocorrelation-preserving
surrogates to ensure that the traveling waves corresponding to the different behavioral states are
statistically robust. To do this, we circularly rotated the coordinates of the electrodes for each
stable epoch and passed these shuffled wave patterns into our SCICA approach and subjected the
corresponding results to MANOVA to estimate the f-statistics for these shuffled wave patterns.
Surrogates tests are powerful non-parametric tests that are adaptive to the data in consideration,
and highly robust to the specific distribution of the data, therefore reducing Type I and Type II
statistical errors usually found in parametric tests. F-statistics from empirical data are then
compared to this histogram of f-statistics and then significance is assessed based on whether the
empirical data is outside 95% (p < 0.05), 99% (p < 0.01), or 99.9% (p < 0.001), of the histogram.
Note that this shuffling preserves the spatial autocorrelation of the wave patterns, but destroys
the specific structure associated with them, therefore destroying the systematic relationship
between the wave direction and task state. We then constructed the histogram of the f-statistics
of these surrogates and then compared the empirically estimated f-statistics to this surrogate
distribution. This analysis revealed that our results were highly significant across all clusters (all
p’s < 0.001).

(iv) Assessing group-level significance
For assessing statistical significance for the group level results related to fraction of wave
strength and fraction of significance (Figures 4, 7-9, Supplementary Figure 19), we used chi-
squared tests with FDR-corrections for multiple comparisons (p < 0.05) across frequencies
(theta/alpha and beta) and hemispheres (left and right).

(v) Control analysis to assess the effects of oscillation frequency on behavior
To rule out the possibility that the behavioral results could be driven by changes in spectral
content (e.g., oscillation frequency), we ran the CICA analysis on the frequency contents of each
episode. Specifically, we estimated the peak frequency for each trial and electrode separately,
and then passed these measures to the same CICA and MANOVA analysis as in our wave
analysis approach. However, this analysis revealed that the spectral contents do not differ
between any of the task periods in the spatial task or any of the letters in the verbal task (all p’s >
0.05), indicating that the effects that we observed cannot be explained by differences in spectral
contents, rather they are related to the traveling waves.

We also carried out additional analysis by passing the peak frequencies during different tasks to
train our neural network decoder to distinguish pairwise behavioral states. As before, we used
our shuffling analysis procedure by shuffling the labels of the behavioral states such as encoding,
retrieval, etc. and then running the same decoding analysis on this shuffled data to generate a
distribution of shuffled data against which the actual decoding performance can then be
compared. However, we could not decode the behavioral states by using the peak frequencies,
neither in the spatial task nor in the verbal task (all p’s > 0.05). This suggests that the decoding
performance is driven by the different wave patterns that we observed across behaviors, and not
driven by a difference in peak frequencies across different task conditions. These new results
reinforce the fact that the effects that we observed cannot be explained by differences in peak
frequencies, rather they are related to the traveling waves.

(vi) Control analysis to assess the effects of filtering
Since our oscillation detection algorithm is based on identifying peaks in the power spectrum
which is averaged across trials, we carried out a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) analysis to ensure
that these oscillations are actually present at the individual stable epoch level. Specifically, we
concatenated all the filtered recordings at the oscillation frequency and raw recordings across all
the stable epochs for each cluster and then calculated the Pearson correlation between the filtered
and raw data. This analysis revealed that the correlation values are statistically significant across
all clusters (median Pearson r ~ 0.6, all p’s < 0.001). These high correlation coefficients indicate
that the narrowband filtered signals are capturing a large amount of signal in the raw recording,
showing that the filtering procedure is capturing a dominant amount of variance in the
recordings.

Moreover, we also ran our SNR analysis for the different wave modes such as planar, rotational,
concentric, and complex, to examine whether the SNR differs for the different wave modes. We
first classified each stable epoch as one of the modes (planar/rotational/concentric/complex)
based on the magnitude of the activation function, i.e., a stable epoch was classified as a planar
wave if the magnitude of the activation function corresponding to the planar mode was the
highest, etc. We then concatenated the filtered and raw recordings across all the stable epochs for
each mode and calculated the Pearson correlations between the filtered and raw data for each
mode. We then compared the correlations for the pairwise modes (planar vs. rotational, planar
vs. concentric, rotational vs. concentric, etc.) for each oscillation cluster. This analysis revealed
that the correlation values for the pairwise modes do not differ from each other in any cluster (all
p’s > 0.05, Mann-Whitney U-test). This suggests that the different wave patterns that we
observed in our data are not driven by a difference in SNR.

To rule out the possibility that the effects could be driven by changes in SNR, we calculated the
Pearson correlation between the filtered and raw data for each of the behavioral states separately,
both for the spatial memory and verbal memory tasks. We then used these correlation values in
our neural network decoding analysis to distinguish pairwise behavioral states. As before, we
used our shuffling analysis procedure by shuffling the labels of the behavioral states such as
encoding, retrieval, etc. and then running the same decoding analysis on this shuffled data to
generate a distribution of shuffled data against which the actual decoding performance can then
be compared. However, we could not decode pairwise behavioral states by using these
correlation values (all p’s > 0.05). This suggests that the decoding performance is driven by the
different wave patterns that we observed across behaviors, and not driven by a difference in SNR
across different task conditions.

Decoding analysis of the relation between traveling waves and behavior
Our final goal was to test whether we could decode the broad and specific behavioral states from
the diverse traveling wave patterns in our datasets. Decoding behavioral states in our datasets is a
multiclass classification problem. We converted this problem into a series of binary classification
tasks, as these can be solved straightforwardly with various multivariate algorithms. We trained
multilayer neural networks (Bernardi et al., 2020), with cross-validation, for classifying pairwise
behavioral states (for example, encoding versus retrieval, letter “D” versus letter “J”, etc.),
separately for the spatial and verbal memory tasks, training a neural network classifier for each
oscillation cluster separately. We used a PyTorch-based four-layer neural network for this binary
classification problem (Paszke et al., 2019). We used the extracted weights from the CICA
procedure as features for training our neural network classifiers. We observed that increasing the
number of modes for training increased the network test decoding accuracy (Figure 10B).
Therefore, we included all the modes for classifying the behavioral states. Also please note that
the higher order modes (modes beyond 6) were mostly complex wave shapes and, these higher
order modes progressively contributed less to the test decoding accuracy (Figure 10B), indicating
lack of specific wave structure in these higher order modes compared to the lower order modes
(modes lower than 6).

The multilayer network architecture comprised an input layer, two hidden layers (32 and 16
neurons respectively), and an output layer with a sigmoid activation function, similar to the
neural network architectures previously used for classifying behavioral states (Bernardi et al.,
2020). The inputs for all our decoding analysis were the activation functions or the weights since
for a given mode, these were changing across different task periods. Please note that for a grid
with “N” number of electrodes and hence “N” number of dimensions in CICA, a 2N dimensional
neural network was trained (the factor 2 comes from the fact that the weights are complex
numbers and hence real and imaginary parts were considered separately). ReLU activation
functions were applied to the hidden layers to introduce nonlinearity and improve generalization
(Dahl et al., 2013). The network architectures were kept the same across the spatial and verbal
memory datasets, and individual models were trained for each oscillation cluster separately to
optimize neural network hyperparameters. To further enhance generalization, dropout
regularization was implemented after each hidden layer (Srivastava et al., 2014). For model
optimization, we used Binary Cross Entropy as the loss function, ideal for binary classification
tasks (Ruby & Yendapalli, 2020), and the Adam optimizer during training (Paszke et al., 2019).
To ensure robust optimization and generalization, we employed cross-validation for iterative
training over multiple epochs. For each pair of behavioral states, we first rebalanced the data
such that we have an equal number of epochs per behavioral state (van Gerven et al., 2013). We
used a five-fold cross-validation technique in which the network model was fitted on 80% of the
data and then its performance was tested on the remaining 20%. We used a subsampling
procedure where each epoch was randomly assigned to a particular fold, subject to the constraint
that all behavioral states are evenly represented (van Gerven et al., 2013), and then averaged the
network decoding accuracies across folds.

To access group level statistical significance for the decoding accuracy results, we used one-
sided sign tests versus chance (p < 0.05). Moreover, we also carried out additional statistical
analysis by shuffling the labels of the behavioral states such as encoding, retrieval, etc. and then
running the same decoding analysis on this shuffled data to generate a distribution of shuffled
data against which the actual decoding performance can then be compared. This analysis
revealed that our decoding results are statistically significant across all clusters (all p’s < 0.05),
suggesting that structure of wave activity is the source of the classification accuracy.

Please note that all our traveling waves analysis were carried out for each cluster and subject
separately since each cluster showed specific patterns of wave strength and directions, which
differed across clusters and subjects. Due to the variability of the strength and directions of the
traveling waves, our decoder was also run in each cluster separately rather than collapsing across
subjects (Figure 10, Supplementary Figure 20). Group level results are finally shown in Figure 4
and Supplementary Figure 19 to compare the wave-strength for different types of waves and task
periods.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors relate traveling wave propagation in the human brain (ECoG, epilepsy patients) to behavior (spatial and verbal
memory tasks). Traveling waves were defined as propagated oscillations at fixed frequency. Procedure: 1) Find an
oscillation at a single frequency that is present simultaneously on multiple electrodes; 2) Identify a contiguous cluster of
electrodes with oscillations at the same frequency; 3) Find a systematic propagation of phase across this cluster of
electrodes. Their approach identifies waves that last ~80-180 ms and form complex patterns, such as spirals, sources and
sinks, besides simpler plane waves. They also used Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to identify and quantify the
wave patterns into modes and detect how much each mode was present at any given time. Results were validated using
simulations.
Results:
Average of 6 significant modes, explaining > 80% of variance (first three explained ~34%, ~19%, ~10% = ~64%). Found
differential presence of patterns across hemispheres during tasks. Concentric waves also differed between spatial and
verbal tasks. Waves had significant shifts in direction or strength between stages of the spatial memory task. Waves also
often changed direction or strength for individual letters in the verbal memory task. Behavioral states could be "reliably"
decoded (~60% accuracy, chance at 50% -- achieved ~70% with ~20 modes) for the spatial memory task. Some states were
better distinguishable by the decoder than others, and this correlates with how distinguishable their wave patterns were.
Letters were also decoded (~50-70% accuracy, depending on the letters being compared; chance at 50%), and again this
was correlated with how distinguishable their wave patterns were.
Critique:
The paper presents a study on traveling waves in humans during task and show that diverse patterns of traveling waves are
not only present but also correlate with behavior. The conclusions are backed up by the results and methods look sound.
1. It is worth noting that a lot of the work is based on previous studies, including some from the same authors. This raises the
problem that the novelty of the current study simply arises from applying their established approach to their new datasets.
2. I would like to see the figure legends be more descriptive. Often, I could not fully understand what was being plotted (e.g.,
Fig. 1i and SFig. 4c).
3. Decoding numbers are relatively low, but I'm not sure if one would expect much better given the info fed and model used.
However, the authors should soften the claims of "reliable" and "robust" decoding.
4. The description of modes and their relation to wave patterns could be clarified more, it feels like modes are essentially
capturing pattern types, but modes and pattern types are used on different results back and forth.

### Reviewer 2

This is a technically rigorous, data-rich study that provides a detailed taxonomy of wave patterns observed during memory
tasks. A comprehensive set of controls was implemented to identify traveling waves and link them to behavioral states.
While the analyses are thorough and address potential confounds in depth, I believe the manuscript would benefit from a
broader examination of the functional role of these patterns to better suit the broad readership of Nature Communications.
Limitations:
The reliance on pairwise classification appears methodologically restrictive. Although the authors suggest that their analysis
of traveling waves may yield novel insights into the brain’s spatial organization, it is not evident how binary discrimination
alone substantiates this claim. Complex neural datasets frequently exhibit nonlinear decision boundaries and latent
structure, such as the hierarchical organization observed in episodic memory tasks. Capturing such complexity may require
targeted feature engineering and model architectures that explicitly accommodate multi-class or structured outputs.
Moreover, performance in a binary framework does not imply that the learned feature representations will generalize to the
multi-class setting necessary for comprehensive behavioral decoding, which appears to be the broader aim of this work.
Approaches employing deeper architectures or ensemble methods may be more appropriate for uncovering meaningful
structure in the data. In the absence of such methods, it is difficult to assess the strength of the assertion that “behavioral
states of human memory representations can be decoded from traveling waves.” Given that MANOVA has already
demonstrated statistically significant differences between states, the added value of the multi-layer network analysis remains
unclear.
Also, a key limitation is the omission of spike rate analyses. Claims that waves “dynamically strengthen” or “transiently
reorganize” functional connectivity or route spiking should be supported by spike–field coherence or spike rate comparisons
across the new wave patterns (e.g. "complex waves") considered here.
I would appreciate a more detailed discussion of the potential mechanisms underlying the predominance of one wave class
over another. For instance, the observation that source waves are more prevalent in the spatial memory task is intriguing and
could potentially reflect changes in inhibitory dynamics and reorganization of the theta cycle between encoding and
retrieval. Similarly, rotating waves might arise from spatial inhomogeneities, but it is unclear why such factors would
specifically influence the spatial memory task more than the verbal task (Fig. 4).
Last, the potential impact of array positioning on the observed results is unclear. For instance, could the detected plane
waves represent segments of larger rotating waves, and if so, how was this possibility addressed? Likewise, could the
observed complex wave patterns be artifacts rather than planar or rotating waves?

### Reviewer 4

This paper is devoted to measuring and classifying waves of activity in the human brain performing tasks. The key results
are that there are many different kinds of such waves, and that these kinds, which can be complex, change in a predictable
way in the course of carrying out a task. The authors interpret their results to imply that these waves have structure that can
give insights into cognition, such as memory.
Much of the paper is highly technical and, to this reader, very difficult to get through. The basic kinds of simple patters (plane
waves, sources, sinks, spirals inward, spirals outward) are easy to understand. But the data present more complex
phenomena, and a lot of effort is given to choosing data that can represent “stable epochs” and then using ICA to classify the
stable epochs in terms of simpler phenomena. I did not understand the details of what they were trying to do (e.g., with
“activation functions”). It didn’t help that static pictures don’t fully capture movements in a dynamic pattern. I did try to look up
some videos with links in the paper; I got a message that they were too big to run on my computer.
However, their big message did come through: the dynamic structure of these patterns contains information that reflect
cognitive states. That some aspects can reflect broad cognitive states has been argued in previous papers of this group and
that of Earl Miller and collaborators. For example, it is argued in previous papers that some plane waves associated with
learning go in the opposite direction from waves associated with recall. This makes perfect sense functionally, since the
regions of the brain participating in learning or recall might be involved in temporally opposing manners in the two functions.
However, this paper makes the further claim that these waves can contain information about very specific information in
memory, such as telling one letter of the alphabet from another. They also suggest that other types of waves (non-planar)
may also be associated with function. As I explain below, these assertions seem unlikely to me and suggests to me that the
phenomena associated with such specific items and some kinds of non-planar waves may be epiphenomena: there are
associations, but the associations do not reflect cognitive causality. The very interesting result of this paper that the nature of
the waves changes over the course of a single trial of an experiment does not, for me, constitute a support for the functional
use of all of the waves. However, I should note that the paper does not claim that the waves are important for coding, only for
decoding, which may be consistent with epiphenomena and interesting by itself.
My intuition about the use of waves such as “targets” come from the chemical experiments in which such traveling waves
were found, namely the “Belousov Zhabotinsky” solution, a chemical solution that oscillates between red and blue when it is
stirred. In a thin layer (and covered to prevent convection) it creates patterns of outwardly going targets that continue to
change in time. For me, the essential point here is that the centers of these targets are random in space. If the target patterns
in the brain are produced by a similar mechanism, it is hard to see how such an unregulated pattern could be of use in any
highly regulated function. The spiral patterns in the BZ solution have centers that correspond to some heterogeneity, so
maybe it is possible for them to be somewhat regulated. However, I’m finding it very hard to imagine a situation in a wave
(even a planar wave) corresponds to a letter of the alphabet. Since the latter is learned, what kind of learning rule would set
up a wave?
What I would have liked to see is a deeper discussion of why the authors think that the new patterns they found, (e.g., the
targets and spirals) actually contribute to cognitive processing, as opposed to being associated with processing. One of the
authors is a world class expert on such patterns and may have thought more about this than is in the paper. I would also like
to have seen a deeper discussion of the cited modeling paper by Bhattacharya et al, since the authors of the current paper
say that they reproduce the results of that paper experimentally. Do they think their waves come from thalamocortical
interactions, as in the Bhattacharya et al paper? These might to be very different from the BZ patterns and perhaps subject to
more specific regulation than the latter.
The data they found should certainly be published somewhere, but lack of a link, even hypothetical, to some possible
mechanisms for producing the patterns and linking those mechanisms to cognition makes the paper less exciting. If they
think that possible decoding functions constitute the importance of the paper, that should be expanded upon.

We thank the reviewer for raising these issues. The main goal of our decoding analysis was not to
propose targeted neural network architectures, rather to demonstrate a proof-of-concept framework for
traveling waves which can be used as a basis for single trial neural decoding, and therefore can be
potentially used as a tool to develop a novel brain-computer-interface. Please note that our decoding
analysis using multilayer neural networks, even though carried out for pair-wise cortical states, employs
rigorous cross-validation procedures to ensure robust decoding and avoid any overtraining. We used the
extracted weights from the ICA procedure as features for training our neural network classifiers and we
included all the modes for classifying the behavioral states. Multilayer neural networks are capable of
handling highly nonlinear and high-dimensional decision boundaries and latent structure, such as the
hierarchical organization observed in our complex spatial episodic memory tasks.
As per the reviewer’s suggestion of multi-class classification, we have now carried out additional
analyses where we have run our neural network analysis for simultaneous decoding of all behavioral
states, where we performed training on all the behavioral states together and then classified the
behavioral states on the test data using the same five-fold cross-validation technique. We were able to
successfully decode the behavioral states for both the spatial (p < 0.001, one-sided sign test, median
decoding accuracy ~ 40% versus chance at 16.66%) and verbal (p < 0.001, one-sided sign test, median
decoding accuracy ~ 15% versus chance at 12.5%) memory tasks in our multiclass decoding analysis.
These multiclass decoding results strongly support our conclusion that behavioral states of human
memory representations can be decoded from traveling waves.
The reviewer also asked about our rationale for the pairwise decoding approach rather than a multi-class
classification approach. Although these two approaches can give analytically similar results (Lorena et
al., 2008), our rationale for focusing on pairwise decoding analysis in the manuscript is that, some pairs
of cortical states were more decodable compared to other pairs. For example, Figure 10C shows that for
cluster 7, the spatial wave patterns for the encoding and distractor periods were distinct from each other
and hence were more easily distinguishable compared to those from the confidence and feedback
periods. Moreover, the navigation and distractor states were generally decodable from other states, but
not from each other, which indicates that these behaviors generally exhibit similar traveling wave
patterns (Figures 10F, G). These important results will be missed from a multiclass decoding analysis
where all the behavioral states are decoded together or, from the MANOVA significance tests where all
the behavioral states are simultaneously included for statistical analysis. Therefore, the focus of our
manuscript’s decoding is the pairwise approach, with rigorous cross-validation procedures to avoid
overtraining, which again strongly supports our conclusion that behavioral states of human memory
representations can be decoded from traveling waves. Moreover, to further justify that the binary
approach is robust, we have now carried out additional statistical analysis by shuffling the labels of the
behavioral states such as encoding, retrieval, etc. and then running the same decoding analysis on this
shuffled data to generate a distribution of shuffled data against which the actual decoding performance
can then be compared. This analysis again revealed that our decoding results are statistically significant
across all clusters (all p’s < 0.05), suggesting that structure of wave activity is the source of the
classification accuracy and behavioral states of human memory representations can be decoded from the
structure of the traveling waves. We have included these new results in the revised version of our
manuscript (page 31).
2.2. Also, a key limitation is the omission of spike rate analyses. Claims that waves “dynamically
strengthen” or “transiently reorganize” functional connectivity or route spiking should be
supported by spike–field coherence or spike rate comparisons across the new wave patterns (e.g.
"complex waves") considered here.
Thank you for this comment. We agree that spike rate or spike-field coherence analysis is interesting
and would directly show how traveling waves modulate and are modulated by the spiking activity of
neurons. However, such an analysis will require us to collect entirely new experimental data
(simultaneous spike data and LFP) from new patients. We believe that this is beyond the scope of the
current manuscript.
Nevertheless, we have now acknowledged this in the Discussion section of our paper (page 14): “Future
studies with simultaneous single neuron and intracranial EEG recordings from neurosurgical patients
performing spatial and verbal memory tasks are needed to directly examine the functional relevance of
the spike-wave coupling. This will reveal how the complex spatial patterns of traveling waves modulate
and are modulated by the spiking activity of the neurons.”
2.3. I would appreciate a more detailed discussion of the potential mechanisms underlying the
predominance of one wave class over another. For instance, the observation that source waves are
more prevalent in the spatial memory task is intriguing and could potentially reflect changes in
inhibitory dynamics and reorganization of the theta cycle between encoding and retrieval. Similarly,
rotating waves might arise from spatial inhomogeneities, but it is unclear why such factors would
specifically influence the spatial memory task more than the verbal task (Fig. 4).
We would like to thank the reviewer for this suggestion. As suggested, we have now added detailed
discussion related to the mechanisms that could underlie different types of traveling waves and their
functional roles.
This new text, in pages 10-11, states: “An especially distinctive aspect of our results concerns concentric
source and sink waves. A previous study showed that source waves were common than sinks during
sleep spindles in humans, indicating that sources putatively support complex cortical processes such as
memory consolidation and synaptic plasticity (Muller et al., 2016). Because they involve waves
propagating outward from a single location, we hypothesize that the source waves we observed indicate
the presence of a small local group of neuronal assemblies that dominate information flow by routing
their information outward from one local area in a direction towards widespread brain areas. Given
that we found an especially large prevalence of source waves in our spatial memory task, it suggests
that spatial cognition involves directed information flow propagating outward from local nodes. Spatial
episodic memory (navigating or recalling spatial layouts) requires broad integration of rich sensory
information across multiple cortical and subcortical areas, which might favor more sources of waves
since these sources involve widespread initiation of oscillatory activity to broadcast information
outward across multiple networks. In comparison to the spatial task, the Sternberg verbal working
memory task, which involves maintaining a few items on each trial that each come from a relatively
small dictionary of possible items, primarily recruits fronto-temporal circuits rather than the larger-
scale brain networks that are important for richer spatial memories. Therefore, the verbal memory task
might rely more on focused convergence of waves onto sinks for more localized cortical processing. In
the verbal memory task, inhibitory control is stronger to limit irrelevant spread; thus, in this context our
results suggest that the oscillations we observed are relevant because they suggest that neural activity
converges onto fewer stable sinks during encoding to help maintain fixed items in buffers. Our findings
and these predictions regarding the functional role of traveling waves and spatial oscillation patterns in
memory are, of course, predictions based on our empirical findings, but they provide useful hypothesis
for computational modeling that may probe the importance of these source nodes for cortical processing
and spatial cognition.
Muller et al., 2016 also found the presence of rotational waves during sleep spindles. Rotational waves
such as spirals revisit the same brain areas in multiple cycles, therefore sequentially scanning
distributed brain areas to help enhance synaptic plasticity for memory consolidation. We observed a
higher number of rotational waves during the spatial memory task compared to the verbal memory task.
Spatial episodic memory requires bidirectional loops between the cortical areas and the subcortical
areas. Rotational waves naturally emerge in recurrent loop topologies where excitatory signals re-enter
the system with delays. These spirals can integrate multimodal spatial signals such as landmarks,
trajectories, and contexts into coherent phase patterns, therefore providing a temporal scaffold for
multiplexing different feature streams around the spiral core and supporting flexible scene construction
and navigation. These features might be less critical for short term verbal working memory which is
more maintenance-oriented, therefore might favor more simple, stable oscillatory attractors such as
planar waves with minimal dynamical complexity.”
2.4. Last, the potential impact of array positioning on the observed results is unclear. For instance,
could the detected plane waves represent segments of larger rotating waves, and if so, how was
this possibility addressed?
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Since the larger 8´8 grids in our dataset span
almost one of the entire hemispheres, it’s highly unlikely that a detected plane wave is part of a larger
rotational wave. But if the size of the ECoG grid is small, such as the 6´4 or 8´4 grids in our dataset,
it is indeed possible that the detected plane waves could represent segments of larger rotating waves.
This is an inherent limitation of our methodology. Therefore, it is theoretically possible that the number of
rotational waves that we detected in our dataset could potentially be undercounted, and we do not
believe there is any analytical method for overcoming this issue.
Nonetheless, to address this issue transparently, we have now acknowledged this limitation on pages 24-
25: “If the size of the ECoG grid is small, such as the 6´4 or 8´4 grids in our dataset, there is a
possibility that the detected planar waves could represent segments of larger rotational waves.
Therefore, the number of rotational waves that we have detected in our dataset could potentially be
undercounted. Future studies with much larger ECoG arrays, or noninvasive whole brain recordings,
could be useful to provide a more accurate assessment of the number of rotational waves and their
functional role during various memory tasks.”
Likewise, could the observed complex wave patterns be artifacts rather than planar or rotating
waves?
Please note that complex waves were those which could not be classified as one of the following
categories: “planar”, “rotational”, or “concentric” (“expanding” or “contracting”). Complex waves were
also stable at the individual epoch level as shown in Figure 9 and also across epochs since these waves
were able to distinguish behavior, for example, see Supplementary Figure 19. Also please note that some
complex waves showed a combination of multiple patterns, such as separate subsets of electrodes
showed planar, rotating, or expanding/contracting waves (Figure 9, Supplementary Figures 9-18). Group
level statistics related to complex waves are in Figure 4 and Supplementary Figure 18.
To ensure that complex waves were statistically robust, only those complex waves that exceeded the
variance explained threshold were included in our analysis (Figure 4 and Supplementary Figure 18).
Specifically, we compared the variance explained for each mode with the theoretical variance threshold
100/n, where n is the number of electrodes in an ECoG grid (please see Methods for details). We
additionally shuffled the electrodes in each cluster and recalculated the variance distribution across
modes and confirmed that the shuffled variance for all modes converged to the theoretical variance
threshold of 100/n. Also, please note that complex waves were subject to the same rigorous statistical
tests as other wave shapes. These complex waves were statistically robust (all p’s < 0.001, Methods,
Figures 1I, Supplementary Figure 2) ruling out the possibility that complex waves are artifacts.
Reviewer #3:
The paper studies how widespread brain regions coordinate their activity to support complex
behaviors, which is a fundamental question in neuroscience. The authors demonstrate the
existence of different types of travelling waves in the human cortex during memory tasks (planar,
spiral, concentric, and complex traveling waves), and show how these specific wave patterns
correlate with and can be used to decode distinct behavioral states. This is a major contribution.
The methodology is clear and robust, especially after the revisions, where various methodological
issues were raised.
Moreover, the authors showed that neither peak oscillation frequency nor SNR could be used to
decode behavioral states, strengthening their conclusion that the observed effects are genuinely
related to the patterns of traveling waves.
Given the novelty of the findings, the methodological rigor, and the comprehensive response to
previous critiques, this paper makes a strong case for publication. It is likely to be of broad
interest to the neuroscience community and to stimulate further research into the functional role
of complex traveling waves in cognition.
Thank you so much for appreciating the significance of our contributions and your very encouraging
words. Please find responses to your specific comments below.
3.1. As a minor comment, in the the section about the generative mechanisms, the authors should
also refer to computational models that describe the appearance of frequency specific activation
patterns (static or travelling) due to axonal time-delays, such as the normalized connectome by
Petkoski & Jirsa 2022 Netw Neurosci, and modelling works for whole-brain activity such as:
Cabral et al. 2023 Nat Comm Biol and Petkoski et al 2019 PTRSA.
Similarly, important are the modeling works on the thalamo-cortical circuits which focus on the
cortical geometry and were developed by the group of Peter Robinson and lately applied by the
lab of Michael Breakspear.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out these important references, which we have now cited at
appropriate places in our manuscript including on page 11: “These locally generated waves can
propagate across widespread regions between locally connected neurons and interact with other locally
generated waves, to generate complex patterns of propagating oscillations (Bao & Wu, 2003; Cabral et
al., 2022; Huang et al., 2010; Jeong et al., 2002; Petkoski & Jirsa, 2019, 2022; Schiff et al., 2007).”,
and also on page 13: “Subcortical generation of traveling waves also hints at the possibility of three-
dimensional traveling waves coordinating neural activity between the cortical and subcortical brain
areas, rather than waves propagating only along the cortical surface. Recent fMRI studies using a new
type of wave mode namely the geometric eigenmode have demonstrated that three dimensional
thalamocortical traveling waves play a critical role in many higher order brain functions (Pang et al.,
2023; Robinson, 2025). Denser sampling of depth electrodes in three-dimensions may help to better
understand the full complexity of the generation and propagation of traveling waves across different
shapes of cortex, perhaps answering the question about how waves propagate across sulci.”
3.2. Finally, as a suggestion to both, the authors and the editor, I find it very difficult to read the
work in this kind of format, with the figures and captions separated. I strongly suggest including a
reader-friendly file with the figures and captions in the text.
For the reviewer’s convenience, we have now uploaded an additional article file namely
“Reader_Friendly_File”, where the figures and captions are in the text.
Reviewer #4:
What I would have liked to see is a deeper discussion of why the authors think that the new
patterns they found, (e.g., the targets and spirals) actually contribute to cognitive processing, as
opposed to being associated with processing. One of the authors is a world class expert on such
patterns and may have thought more about this than is in the paper. I would also like to have seen
a deeper discussion of the cited modeling paper by Bhattacharya et al, since the authors of the
current paper say that they reproduce the results of that paper experimentally. Do they think
their waves come from thalamocortical interactions, as in the Bhattacharya et al paper? These
might to be very different from the BZ patterns and perhaps subject to more specific regulation
than the latter.
The data they found should certainly be published somewhere, but lack of a link, even
hypothetical, to some possible mechanisms for producing the patterns and linking those
mechanisms to cognition makes the paper less exciting. If they think that possible decoding
functions constitute the importance of the paper, that should be expanded upon.
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion related to enhancing the depth of the Discussion on the
mechanisms of the waves and their association with cognitive processing such as the alphabets.
The reviewer wants us to highlight the novel contributions related to the complex wave patterns,
therefore, we want to briefly highlight the novel contributions and the functional relevance of the
complex spatial patterns of traveling waves. In our paper, we have shown the presence of new types of
complex spatial patterns of traveling waves which are associated with both broad and specific behavioral
states, with a specific spatial pattern correlated with a particular behavioral state. Therefore, and as we
have shown in our paper using deep learning models, the behavioral states can be decoded using these
complex spatial patterns of traveling waves. This is a significant advancement over prior studies which
used planar waves and their association with human behavior. Since planar waves travel in only one
direction, it severely limits their ability to rapidly and dynamically reorganize to adapt to complex
behaviors in humans. Our results show that the cortex exhibits heterogeneous patterns of neuronal
activity beyond the previously known anatomical and functional hierarchies from connectomics.
We have now modified our text to further clarify the generative mechanisms of the traveling waves on
page 11 of our revised manuscript: “Our findings converge well with theoretical predictions from
biologically plausible neural models based on weakly coupled oscillators (Bhattacharya et al., 2021;
Sato, 2022). These models hypothesize that complex patterns of waves can be generated locally based
on the initial spatial activation of neurons, where each neuron is connected to a few of its neighbors,
with distance dependent axonal delays in the order of conduction along unmyelinated horizontal fibers
(Davis et al., 2021; Destexhe, 1994; Ermentrout & Kleinfeld, 2001). These locally generated waves can
propagate across widespread regions between locally connected neurons and interact with other locally
generated waves, to generate complex patterns of propagating oscillations (Bao & Wu, 2003; Cabral et
al., 2022; Huang et al., 2010; Jeong et al., 2002; Petkoski & Jirsa, 2019, 2022; Schiff et al., 2007).
In addition to the coupling functions, a key determinant of the shape of these wave patterns is the
presence of local shifts in the frequency of local oscillations. In locally coupled oscillator networks,
waves tend to propagate away from the cortical locations with the fastest intrinsic oscillation
frequencies, following a gradient to the locations with the slowest oscillations (Kopell & Ermentrout,
1990). Thus, local activations of strong or fast oscillations can have a strong influence on the global
topography of these traveling waves (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2010; Sato, 2022). Using
this model, based on the spatial location of the locally generated wave sources and their relative
frequencies, a wide range of stable, regular (non-random) wave patterns can be generated (Kopell &
Ermentrout, 1990).”
We have now also specifically discussed the different generative mechanisms of the specific patterns of
traveling waves on pages 11-12: “For example, a linear spatial gradient in frequencies, such as
relatively higher frequency on the left side of the ECoG array compared to the right side, can lead to a
planar traveling wave going from the left to right on the ECoG array (Ermentrout & Kopell,
1984). Therefore, a presence of a planar traveling wave for a specific English letter would imply this
frequency heterogeneity in the left of the ECoG array compared to the right side represents that specific
English letter. Similarly, bullseyes or target waves can also be generated by frequency gradients using
nearest-neighbor coupled oscillators (Ren & Ermentrout, 1998). For example, a source wave in an
ECoG array can be generated when the frequency at the center of the array is relatively higher
compared to all other places of the ECoG array, constituting a wave diverging away from the center of
the array. Therefore, a presence of a source wave for specific English letter indicates relatively higher
frequency at the center of the ECoG array responsible for cognitive representation for that specific
letter. Similarly, a sink wave in an ECoG array can be generated when the frequency at the center of the
array is lower compared to all other places of the ECoG array, constituting a wave converging to the
center of the array. Therefore, a relatively lower frequency at the center of the array for a specific letter
would indicate that such frequency lowering is causally responsible for cognitively representing that
specific letter. Recently, in a new work, we have found the effect of the frequency heterogeneities on
generating these planar and concentric traveling waves and when these waves are combined with
rotational traveling waves, can produce a wide range of complex traveling waves (Das et al., 2025).
More broadly, our results of distinctive spatial wave patterns for separate memory items suggest that
there are spatial patterns of excitation across the cortex for separate memory items during cognition,
similar to those seen in the hippocampus (Mickiewicz et al., 2025).”
Our revised paper also describes the functional importance of spirals by showing that the existence of a
spiral corresponds to a small group of electrodes at the core of the spiral that have large phase advances
that is functionally relevant for representing an English alphabet as we note on page 12: “Similarly, the
presence of spiral waves is also informative about the spatial arrangement of the cortical pattern that
supports distinct behavioral states. Certain arrangements of spatial heterogeneities in an excitable
media can produce spiral waves. For example, spatial heterogeneity in a 2×2 block of electrodes at
the middle of the ECoG grid where the phase advances by approximately an even ± step along each
edge, such that the four edges together complete an approximate ±2𝜋 winding around the block, can
produce a spiral wave, with the 2×2 block of electrodes at the center constituting the spiral core
(Greenberg & Hastings, 1978). Therefore, a presence of a spiral wave for a specific English letter
indicates a spatial heterogeneity in a 2×2 block of electrodes at the middle of the ECoG array which
constitutes a spiral wave causally responsible for cognitively representing that specific letter.”
The reviewer asked about the Bhattacharya et al. paper, however the goal of our manuscript was not to
reproduce the results of the Bhattacharya et al. paper experimentally. Rather, we mentioned this work to
discuss the interesting question of how three-dimensional waves could be generated in the human
cortex. We now describe this issue more clearly on page 13: “An additional way that traveling waves
could effectively propagate through sulci is by generation in subcortical areas, such as thalamus, as
demonstrated by recent computational modeling work (Bhattacharya et al., 2021) and experimental data
in rodents (Ye et al., 2023). Subcortical generation of traveling waves also hints at the possibility of
three-dimensional traveling waves coordinating neural activity between the cortical and subcortical
brain areas, rather than waves propagating only along the cortical surface.” It is interesting to
speculate about the role of the thalamus in traveling wave generation. However, our dataset did not have
thalamic recordings because typically, neurosurgeons do not put intracranial electrodes in the thalamus.
To directly show the potential impact on the cortical traveling waves from the thalamus, additional data
needs to collected from new epilepsy patients by running the same spatial episodic and verbal memory
tasks, however, we think that such an endeavor is beyond the scope of the current manuscript and we
reserve such work for future exploration.
